test.title: Key Stage 2 Science - Progress Test 2
digitalInstructions: You have 25 minutes for the complete test.
Choose, classify, select, or enter an answer as directed.
Your work is saved automatically on this browser.
Answers and explanations appear only after submission.

attribution.adaptationNote: Response formats were adapted for deterministic digital marking; the assessed science and official mark allocation are preserved.

sections.title: Duck pond
sections.introduction: Peter visits a duck pond with his grandad and his dog. He observes ducks and a mole living near the pond.

questions.originalPrompt: Tick TWO boxes to show two things that are true about a dog and a duck.
questions.adaptedPrompt: Which TWO statements are true about both a dog and a duck?

options.label: They both have fur.
options.feedback: Ducks have feathers rather than fur.

options.label: They both move.
options.feedback: Correct - both animals can move.

options.label: They both lay eggs.
options.feedback: Dogs do not lay eggs.

options.label: They both breathe.
options.feedback: Correct - both animals breathe.

feedback.correct: Correct - both animals move and breathe.
feedback.incorrect: Choose the two life processes shared by both animals.
feedback.explanation: A dog and a duck can both move and breathe. Only the duck lays eggs, and a duck has feathers rather than fur.

questions.adaptationNote: Original exact-two selection preserved.

questions.originalPrompt: Describe how a duck's feet are adapted for swimming.
questions.adaptedPrompt: How are a duck's feet adapted for swimming?

options.label: They are webbed and work like paddles.
options.feedback: Correct - webbed feet push against the water.

options.label: They have sharp claws that grip fish.
options.feedback: Claws do not provide the broad paddle surface needed for swimming.

options.label: They are covered in thick fur.
options.feedback: Ducks do not have fur on their feet.

options.label: They are very small so they do not touch the water.
options.feedback: Swimming feet need to push against the water.

feedback.correct: Correct - webbing makes the feet broad like paddles.
feedback.incorrect: Look for the feature that helps the feet push water backwards.
feedback.explanation: Webbed, broad feet provide a large surface that pushes against the water.

assets.alt: Male and female ducks beside the pond, with the male shown in brighter colours and the female in brown.

questions.adaptationNote: Free response changed to a mark-scheme-supported single choice.

questions.originalPrompt: Why would the female duck be hard to see in a nest?
questions.adaptedPrompt: Why is the female duck hard to see when she is in a nest?

options.label: Her brown colouring blends in with the nest.
options.feedback: Correct - the brown colouring provides camouflage.

options.label: Her bright colours reflect the sunlight.
options.feedback: The female is dull brown rather than brightly coloured.

options.label: She becomes much smaller in the nest.
options.feedback: Her size does not change.

options.label: She cannot make any sound in the nest.
options.feedback: The question is about how difficult she is to see.

feedback.correct: Correct - her colouring camouflages her.
feedback.incorrect: Compare the female's colour with the colours of a nest.
feedback.explanation: The female's dull brown colouring blends into the nest and makes her difficult to see.

assets.alt: Male and female ducks beside the pond, with the male shown in brighter colours and the female in brown.

questions.adaptationNote: Free response changed to a causal single choice.

questions.originalPrompt: Explain why the female duck needs to stay hidden when she is in her nest.
questions.adaptedPrompt: Why does the female duck need to stay hidden in her nest?

options.label: To protect herself and her eggs or ducklings from predators.
options.feedback: Correct - staying hidden reduces the risk from predators.

options.label: To make the pond water warmer.
options.feedback: Hiding in a nest does not warm the pond.

options.label: To make plants grow for food.
options.feedback: Camouflage does not cause plants to grow.

options.label: To change the colour of her feathers.
options.feedback: Her colouring helps her hide; hiding does not change it.

feedback.correct: Correct - hiding helps keep her and her young safe from predators.
feedback.incorrect: Think about animals that might eat the duck, eggs, or ducklings.
feedback.explanation: Camouflage makes the nesting duck less likely to be found by predators or hunters.

questions.adaptationNote: Explanation changed to a causal single choice.

questions.originalPrompt: Describe how a feature of the mole helps the mole to live underground.
questions.adaptedPrompt: Which feature-and-function pair best explains how the mole is adapted to live underground?

options.label: Strong front legs and long claws help it dig through soil.
options.feedback: Correct - the broad, strong front limbs and claws are adapted for digging.

options.label: Large ears help it fly through tunnels.
options.feedback: Moles do not fly, and the pictured ears are not large.

options.label: A flat tail helps it swim across ponds.
options.feedback: The pictured mole is adapted for moving through soil.

options.label: Bright fur produces light underground.
options.feedback: Fur does not produce light.

feedback.correct: Correct - its strong front limbs and claws help it dig.
feedback.incorrect: Choose a visible feature and a function that helps movement through soil.
feedback.explanation: Broad, muscular front limbs and long claws break up and push back soil.

assets.alt: A mole emerging beside a pile of loose soil.

questions.adaptationNote: Feature-plus-explanation response changed to paired single choice.

questions.originalPrompt: Which word cannot be used to describe a mole?
questions.adaptedPrompt: Which word cannot be used to describe a mole?

options.label: Prey
options.feedback: A mole can be prey when it is eaten by another animal.

options.label: Producer
options.feedback: Correct - a mole is an animal and does not make its own food.

options.label: Predator
options.feedback: A mole is a predator when it eats earthworms.

options.label: Consumer
options.feedback: A mole is a consumer because it eats other organisms.

feedback.correct: Correct - a mole is not a producer.
feedback.incorrect: Producers make their own food; animals obtain food by consuming other organisms.
feedback.explanation: A mole can be a predator, prey, and consumer, but not a producer.

questions.adaptationNote: Original single-choice format preserved.

sections.title: Seed dispersal
sections.introduction: Class 6 investigate seeds, how wind carries them, and how seed shape affects the distance travelled.

questions.originalPrompt: Put a cross on the diagram to show where the seed develops.
questions.adaptedPrompt: Select the region of the flower where the seed develops.

image.alt: A black line drawing showing a flower cut open to reveal its reproductive parts.

hotspots.label: Region C
hotspots.answerLabel: Ovary at the base of the flower

feedback.correct: Correct - seeds develop in the ovary at the base of the flower.
feedback.incorrect: Look inside the swollen structure at the base of the flower.
feedback.explanation: After fertilisation, ovules inside the ovary develop into seeds.

questions.adaptationNote: Paper cross changed to an accessible image-hotspot selection.

questions.originalPrompt: What equipment can measure how far the seeds travel?
questions.adaptedPrompt: Which piece of equipment should the children use to measure how far the seeds travel?

options.label: Tape measure
options.feedback: Correct - a tape measure measures distance.

options.label: Thermometer
options.feedback: A thermometer measures temperature.

options.label: Stopwatch
options.feedback: A stopwatch measures time.

options.label: Balance
options.feedback: A balance measures mass.

feedback.correct: Correct - use a tape measure.
feedback.incorrect: Choose equipment designed to measure length or distance.
feedback.explanation: A tape measure, metre rule, ruler, or measuring stick can measure the distance travelled.

assets.alt: A pupil holding a seed in front of an electric fan during a seed-dispersal investigation.

questions.adaptationNote: Free response changed to single choice.

questions.originalPrompt: Explain why the fan helps to make the test fair.
questions.adaptedPrompt: Why does using a fan make the seed-dispersal test fairer than blowing with different children's mouths?

options.label: The fan can provide the same blowing force each time.
options.feedback: Correct - keeping the blowing force consistent controls a variable.

options.label: The fan changes speed randomly each time.
options.feedback: A changing speed would make the comparison less fair.

options.label: The fan makes every seed warmer.
options.feedback: Temperature is not the variable being controlled here.

options.label: The fan measures the distance automatically.
options.feedback: The fan moves air; separate equipment measures distance.

feedback.correct: Correct - the fan provides a consistent force.
feedback.incorrect: A fair comparison keeps the blowing conditions the same.
feedback.explanation: Children may blow with different force or for different lengths of time, while a fan can be kept at one setting.

questions.adaptationNote: Explanation changed to causal single choice.

questions.originalPrompt: Tick ONE box to show which features of the seeds help them to fall slowly.
questions.adaptedPrompt: Which features help a wind-dispersed seed fall slowly?

options.label: Smooth and soft
options.feedback: These features do not necessarily create enough air resistance.

options.label: A large surface area and a low mass
options.feedback: Correct - this combination increases the effect of air resistance.

options.label: A large surface area and a high mass
options.feedback: A high mass makes the seed fall more quickly.

options.label: Flexible and soft
options.feedback: The important features are surface area and mass.

feedback.correct: Correct - a large surface area and low mass slow the fall.
feedback.incorrect: Think about what increases air resistance without adding much weight.
feedback.explanation: A broad, light seed experiences more air resistance compared with its weight and falls more slowly.

assets.alt: A results table comparing sycamore, apple, bulrush, and oak seeds and the distances they travelled.

questions.adaptationNote: Original single-choice format preserved with clarified wording.

questions.originalPrompt: Name the force that slows the seeds as they fall.
questions.adaptedPrompt: Which force slows the seeds as they fall?

options.label: Air resistance
options.feedback: Correct - air resistance opposes the falling motion.

options.label: Gravity
options.feedback: Gravity pulls the seeds down rather than slowing their fall.

options.label: Weight
options.feedback: Weight is the downward force caused by gravity.

options.label: Magnetism
options.feedback: There is no magnetic interaction in this situation.

feedback.correct: Correct - air resistance slows the falling seeds.
feedback.incorrect: Choose the force that opposes movement through air.
feedback.explanation: Air resistance, also called drag, acts opposite to the seed's downward motion.

questions.adaptationNote: One-word response changed to single choice.

questions.originalPrompt: Name ONE other way seeds are dispersed in nature.
questions.adaptedPrompt: Which is another way seeds can be dispersed in nature, apart from wind?

options.label: Animals carry seeds on their fur or after eating fruit.
options.feedback: Correct - animals can transport seeds away from the parent plant.

options.label: Sunlight pulls the seeds across the ground.
options.feedback: Sunlight does not pull seeds across the ground.

options.label: Photosynthesis throws seeds into the air.
options.feedback: Photosynthesis makes sugars; it is not a dispersal mechanism.

options.label: Roots push all seeds into the sky.
options.feedback: Roots do not disperse seeds this way.

feedback.correct: Correct - animals can disperse seeds.
feedback.incorrect: Think about fur, eaten fruit, water, or exploding seed pods.
feedback.explanation: Other accepted methods include animals, water, rolling downhill, and explosive seed pods.

questions.adaptationNote: Open response changed to one mark-scheme-supported method.

sections.title: Grass heads
sections.introduction: Class 6 grow grass on model heads and change one condition at a time to investigate plant growth and water movement.

questions.originalPrompt: Name TWO other things that all plants need to grow.
questions.adaptedPrompt: Apart from water, which TWO things can plants need for healthy growth?

options.label: Light
options.feedback: Accepted - plants need light for photosynthesis.

options.label: Air
options.feedback: Accepted - plants exchange gases with the air.

options.label: Mineral nutrients
options.feedback: Accepted - plants need mineral nutrients for healthy growth.

options.label: Suitable warmth
options.feedback: Accepted - plant processes need a suitable temperature.

options.label: Food supplied by an animal
options.feedback: Plants make sugars by photosynthesis rather than eating animal food.

options.label: A sealed plastic covering
options.feedback: A plastic covering is not a universal requirement for plant growth.

feedback.correct: Correct - both selected requirements are accepted.
feedback.incorrect: Select two genuine plant requirements rather than materials used in this investigation.
feedback.explanation: The mark scheme accepts light, air, mineral nutrients, and suitable warmth, among other scientifically valid responses.

assets.alt: A grass head before planting and after one week, when grass has grown from seeds in its top.

questions.adaptationNote: Open response changed to exact-two selection from accepted and distractor options.

questions.originalPrompt: Give ONE reason why the grass under the hat might look more yellow.
questions.adaptedPrompt: Why might the grass growing under the paper hat look more yellow?

options.label: The hat blocks light from reaching the grass.
options.feedback: Correct - the covered grass receives less light.

options.label: The hat gives the grass much more water.
options.feedback: The amount of water is kept the same.

options.label: The hat creates extra air for the grass.
options.feedback: The hat does not create air.

options.label: The ruler makes the grass yellow.
options.feedback: Measuring height does not cause the colour change.

feedback.correct: Correct - the hat reduces the light reaching the grass.
feedback.incorrect: Think about which condition the paper hat changes.
feedback.explanation: With less light, less chlorophyll may develop and the grass can appear yellow.

questions.adaptationNote: Explanation changed to causal single choice.

questions.originalPrompt: Write yes or no next to each idea to show if it is a good way to measure the height of the grass each week.
questions.adaptedPrompt: Classify each measuring idea as a good method or a bad method.

items.label: Find the average length of several pieces of grass.
Measure a different single piece of grass each week.

feedback.correct: Correct - average several pieces, and do not switch to a different single piece each week.
feedback.incorrect: A reliable method should represent the whole grass head and be repeatable.
feedback.explanation: An average reduces the effect of unusually short or long blades. Measuring a different blade each week creates an unfair comparison.

questions.adaptationNote: Original yes/no grid uses explicit good-method and bad-method choices.

questions.originalPrompt: Tick ONE box to explain why droplets of water form on the inside of the plastic bag.
questions.adaptedPrompt: Why do water droplets form on the inside of the sealed plastic bag?

options.label: Water evaporates from the grass head and condenses on the bag.
options.feedback: Correct - water vapour cools and condenses on the plastic.

options.label: Water condenses from the grass head and evaporates on the bag.
options.feedback: The changes of state are in the wrong order.

options.label: Water dissolves from the grass head and evaporates on the bag.
options.feedback: Dissolving is not the process that releases water vapour here.

options.label: Water dissolves from the grass head and condenses on the bag.
options.feedback: Water first evaporates from the moist grass head.

feedback.correct: Correct - water evaporates, then condenses on the cooler bag.
feedback.incorrect: Follow the water from the moist grass head into the air and then onto the plastic.
feedback.explanation: Liquid water becomes vapour by evaporation and then becomes liquid droplets again by condensation.

assets.alt: A grass head enclosed in a transparent plastic bag with moisture visible inside.

questions.adaptationNote: Original single-choice format preserved.

sections.title: Smallpox
sections.introduction: Dr Edward Jenner investigated whether having cowpox could protect people from smallpox, a disease that could be fatal.

questions.originalPrompt: What sort of statement did Dr Jenner make?
questions.adaptedPrompt: What type of scientific statement was Jenner's idea that people who had cowpox would not catch smallpox?

options.label: Explanation
options.feedback: An explanation accounts for why something happens; Jenner stated what he expected to happen.

options.label: Prediction
options.feedback: Correct - the statement predicts a future outcome that can be tested.

options.label: Comparison
options.feedback: The statement is testable but is not itself a comparison.

options.label: Observation
options.feedback: An observation records what has already been noticed.

feedback.correct: Correct - it was a prediction.
feedback.incorrect: A prediction says what someone expects will happen in a test.
feedback.explanation: Jenner proposed a testable outcome: previous cowpox infection would prevent smallpox.

assets.alt: A historical portrait of Dr Edward Jenner beside his statement about cowpox and smallpox.

questions.adaptationNote: Original single-choice format preserved.

questions.originalPrompt: Describe what Dr Jenner must have done next and also describe the evidence needed to show that his statement was true.
questions.adaptedPrompt: Choose Jenner's required next step and the evidence that would support his prediction.

choices.label: Expose or infect James with smallpox.

feedback.correct: Correct - both the next step and supporting evidence are identified.
feedback.incorrect: One mark is available for the correct next step and one for the correct evidence.
feedback.explanation: Jenner had to expose James to smallpox; if James did not develop the disease, that outcome supported the prediction.

questions.adaptationNote: Two-part explanation changed to a structured response with one mark per correct part.

questions.originalPrompt: Why did Dr Jenner test other people?
questions.adaptedPrompt: Why did Jenner repeat the test with other people?

options.label: To collect more evidence and check that the result was reliable.
options.feedback: Correct - repetition checks whether the result is consistent.

options.label: To make James's original test a fair test.
options.feedback: Repeating with people primarily improves reliability, not fairness.

options.label: To make the prediction change each time.
options.feedback: The same prediction should be tested repeatedly.

options.label: To guarantee the answer he wanted.
options.feedback: A scientific test should not be designed to force a preferred result.

feedback.correct: Correct - testing more people improves reliability.
feedback.incorrect: Think about why scientists repeat tests and collect more data.
feedback.explanation: Repeating the investigation checks that the first result was not unusual and that different people show a similar pattern.

questions.adaptationNote: Explanation changed to causal single choice.

questions.originalPrompt: How many people who were 30 years old died from smallpox?
questions.adaptedPrompt: According to the table, how many 30-year-olds died from smallpox?

feedback.correct: Correct - the table shows 98 deaths at age 30.
feedback.incorrect: Read across the row for age 30.
feedback.explanation: The value paired with age 30 in the table is 98.

assets.alt: A table of smallpox deaths in London in 1844 for ages 10 to 80 at ten-year intervals.

questions.adaptationNote: Original numeric response preserved.

questions.originalPrompt: Explain why Holly cannot be sure of her conclusion.
questions.adaptedPrompt: Why can Holly not be sure that younger people were always more likely to die of smallpox?

options.label: The data do not follow that pattern at every age: more 20-year-olds died than 10-year-olds, and more 60-year-olds than 50-year-olds.
options.feedback: Correct - both comparisons contradict a simple younger-means-more pattern.

options.label: Exactly the same number died at every age.
options.feedback: The values in the table are not all the same.

options.label: The table gives no ages at all.
options.feedback: The table lists ages from 10 to 80.

options.label: The table only contains predictions about future deaths.
options.feedback: The table records deaths that occurred in 1844.

feedback.correct: Correct - the pattern has clear exceptions.
feedback.incorrect: Compare age 10 with 20 and age 50 with 60.
feedback.explanation: A confident conclusion also requires knowing the total number of people at each age, because raw death counts are not the same as likelihood.

assets.alt: A table of smallpox deaths in London in 1844 for ages 10 to 80 at ten-year intervals.

questions.adaptationNote: Explanation changed to an evidence-based single choice.
